title: List.of, Set.of, Map.of: Java 9 immutable factories vs Collections.unmodifiableList
keyPoints: List.of(), Set.of(), and Map.of() (Java 9) create truly immutable collections that reject all modification attempts with UnsupportedOperationException.
These factory methods do not allow null elements or keys; passing null throws NullPointerException.
Collections.unmodifiableList() creates an unmodifiable view, not a truly immutable collection: the underlying mutable list can still change and the view reflects those changes.
List.copyOf() (Java 10) creates an immutable defensive copy that is independent of the source collection.
Set.of() throws IllegalArgumentException if duplicate elements are passed.
Map.of() accepts up to 10 key-value pairs directly; Map.ofEntries() with Map.entry() handles any number.
Immutable collections use compact internal representations with less memory than standard ArrayList or HashMap.

s1_definition.oneliner: Java 9 factory methods (List.of, Set.of, Map.of) create truly immutable collections with no nulls, while Collections.unmodifiableList creates only an unmodifiable view that still reflects changes to the underlying mutable list.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **List.of(), Set.of(), Map.of()** – Java 9 factory methods that return truly immutable collections; all mutating operations throw `UnsupportedOperationException`; null elements throw `NullPointerException`
- **Collections.unmodifiableList()** – wraps a mutable list in a read-only view; the view rejects modification, but the original mutable list can still be changed and the view reflects those changes
- **List.copyOf()** – Java 10 method that creates an immutable defensive copy; independent of the source collection; if the source is already immutable, returns the same instance
- **Compact representation** – immutable collections use optimised internal classes (List12, ListN, Set12, SetN) that consume less memory than ArrayList or HashMap
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, List.of() is like a bank statement carved in stone. No one can add, remove, or change any transaction line. Collections.unmodifiableList() is like a glass display case around the original paper ledger. The display case prevents viewers from touching the ledger, but the accountant (who has the original) can still write in it, and the display reflects the changes. List.copyOf() is like making a photocopy and locking it in a vault. Even if the original ledger changes, the vault copy remains unchanged.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  List.of() vs Collections.unmodifiableList() vs List.copyOf()
  =============================================================

  List.of("SAV2001", "CUR3001"):
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ ImmutableList         │
  │ [SAV2001, CUR3001]   │  No backing mutable reference
  │ add/set/remove: UOE  │  Truly immutable
  └──────────────────────┘

  Collections.unmodifiableList(original):
  ┌──────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ UnmodifiableList VIEW │ ──▶ │ ArrayList (original)  │
  │ add/set/remove: UOE  │      │ Mutable! Can change! │
  └──────────────────────┘      └──────────────────────┘
  Changes to original are visible through the view!

  List.copyOf(original):
  ┌──────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ ImmutableList (copy)  │      │ ArrayList (original)  │
  │ [SAV2001, CUR3001]   │      │ Can change freely    │
  │ Independent of source │      │ No effect on copy    │
  └──────────────────────┘      └──────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Java 9 factory methods (List.of, Set.of, Map.of) create truly immutable collections that reject all modification, prohibit null elements, and use compact internal representations. They are the preferred way to create constant lists, sets, and maps in modern Java. Collections.unmodifiableList is a weaker guarantee: it creates a read-only view, but the underlying mutable collection can still change and those changes are visible through the view.

List.copyOf (Java 10) bridges the gap: it creates an immutable defensive copy from any collection, independent of the source. For collections that are already immutable, copyOf returns the same instance as an optimisation.

In the National Bank of India's API layer, Pankaj established a rule that all service methods return List.copyOf or List.of for response data. This ensured that callers could never accidentally modify the internal state of the service, and that the returned collections were inherently thread-safe for concurrent consumers.

Remember one sentence: use List.of for immutable constants, List.copyOf for defensive copies, and avoid Collections.unmodifiableList in new code because it is a leaky view, not truly immutable.
